paragraphs: Partial-label learning trains a classifier from examples that each have several possible labels, with exactly one assumed to be correct. The central problem is deciding which candidate to trust while learning from the same ambiguous data. Earlier probabilistic approaches can require substantial computation, while newer deep learning methods often use substitute objectives and heuristic updates to resolve labels.

This paper proposes learning a probability distribution over the true label directly through amortized variational inference. A neural network predicts the parameters of an approximate label posterior from the input. Sharing this inference procedure across examples makes probabilistic label disambiguation efficient, rather than requiring a separate intensive inference process for every instance.

The framework accommodates different neural network architectures, connecting scalable prediction with an explicit treatment of label uncertainty. The authors report theoretical support and state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency on synthetic and real-world datasets. These results support probabilistic inference as a practical approach to ambiguous supervision under the setting’s one-correct-candidate assumption.
icml-2026-amortized-variational-inferenc.tldr: A neural variational inference framework efficiently resolves ambiguous candidate labels while achieving reported state-of-the-art classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Shapley values assign credit to contributors, supporting tasks such as feature attribution and data valuation. Computing them exactly is generally intractable, so practical methods estimate them from sampled evaluations. Pairing samples often reduces estimation error, but the reason this common technique works has lacked a clear theoretical explanation.

The paper proves that Shapley values depend exclusively on the odd component of the underlying set function. It further shows that paired sampling makes the regression objective orthogonal to the irrelevant even component, filtering that component out. This identifies which mathematical structure an estimator needs to recover and which structure can be excluded.

The resulting estimator, OddSHAP, fits a polynomial only within the odd subspace. A Fourier basis isolates that subspace, while a proxy model identifies influential interactions to avoid the combinatorial growth associated with higher-order approximations. OddSHAP is consistent, and the reported benchmarks show state-of-the-art estimation accuracy at larger sampling budgets. That sampling-budget qualification is part of the empirical finding.
icml-2026-an-odd-estimator-for-shapley-v.tldr: OddSHAP estimates Shapley values using only the mathematically relevant odd component, achieving leading accuracy at larger sampling budgets.

paragraphs: Constraining a Transformer’s Lipschitz constant limits how strongly its outputs can respond to changes in its inputs. This provides a principled route toward stability and robustness. The theoretical challenge is establishing that architectures built to obey such constraints can still represent the functions they need to learn.

The paper constructs in-context Transformers whose attention and multilayer perceptron blocks take the form of explicit Euler steps along negative gradient flows. This gives both kinds of block a shared dynamical interpretation and builds Lipschitz continuity into the architecture. The construction supports an analysis of stability together with expressive capacity.

The authors prove universal approximation within a Lipschitz-constrained function space. Their formulation treats Transformers as operators on probability measures, which makes the approximation guarantees independent of the number of tokens. The result establishes expressivity within the stated constrained space while preserving the architecture’s continuity properties. It supplies a theoretical foundation for designing stable Transformers without making token count the organizing variable of the guarantee.
icml-2026-approximation-theory-for-lipsc.tldr: The paper constructs Lipschitz-continuous Transformers and proves token-count-independent universal approximation within a Lipschitz-constrained function space.

paragraphs: Language models often direct unusually large amounts of attention toward the first token, a pattern called an attention sink. Several attention variants address this behavior, but their relationships have remained incompletely understood. This paper connects the sink to another observed pattern: only a fixed subset of attention heads contributes to generation.

Through theoretical and empirical analysis, the authors show that sinks in Vanilla Attention and Sink Attention naturally create a mixture-of-experts mechanism inside attention layers. This interpretation explains head collapse in terms of how contributions are distributed across heads. It gives a common perspective on behavior that otherwise appears to be an isolated attention anomaly.

The proposed training method adds an auxiliary loss that balances head loads while accounting for sinks. Experiments report more balanced contributions and improved model performance across Vanilla Attention, Sink Attention, and Gated Attention. The practical contribution is a training intervention informed by the analysis; the conceptual contribution is recognizing an inherent expert-like structure within attention itself.
icml-2026-attention-sink-forges-native-m.tldr: Interpreting attention sinks as an internal mixture-of-experts mechanism motivates a load-balancing loss that reduces head collapse and improves performance.

paragraphs: Code-as-Policy agents control robots by generating executable programs. Their apparent competence can depend heavily on the human-designed operations those programs invoke. CaP-X provides a framework for examining that dependence and improving agents across different levels of control abstraction, interaction, and access to visual information.

CaP-Gym lets agents synthesize and execute programs combining perception and control primitives. CaP-Bench uses this environment to evaluate models systematically. Across 12 models, success improves when human-crafted abstractions are available and declines when they are removed. Additional test-time computation, including repeated interaction, execution feedback, visual differencing, skill synthesis, and ensembled reasoning, can improve robustness even with low-level primitives.

These observations motivate CaP-Agent0, a training-free framework reporting near human-level reliability on several simulated and real manipulation tasks. A further component, CaP-RL, explores reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and supports simulation-to-reality transfer through a shared code-based action interface. Together, the components connect controlled evaluation with concrete ways to strengthen embodied coding agents.
icml-2026-cap-x-a-framework-for-benchmar.tldr: CaP-X measures how robot coding agents depend on human scaffolding and develops interaction and training methods to improve their reliability.

paragraphs: This clustering problem selects facilities as centers and assigns clients to them while respecting facility capacities and demographic selection bounds. Groups may overlap, and each group specifies a minimum and maximum number of selected centers. The objective combines these requirements with minimizing a k-median or k-means clustering cost.

The paper strengthens existing hardness results by showing that severe inapproximability remains even when satisfying the demographic bounds alone is trivial. Thus, difficulty persists in the combined clustering task beyond simply finding a fair selection. The result holds even for tree metrics and when the number of groups grows only logarithmically with the facility set.

For a constant number of groups, the authors give polynomial-time approximation factors of O(log k) for k-median and O(log² k) for k-means. They also obtain constant-factor approximations in time fixed-parameter tractable in k. These guarantees match the best bounds for capacitated clustering without fairness constraints. The polynomial-time algorithms additionally demonstrate practical solvability for instances of modest size.
icml-2026-capacitated-fair-range-cluster.tldr: The paper strengthens hardness results for fair capacitated clustering and provides approximation algorithms when the number of demographic groups is constant.

paragraphs: Entropy control influences how concentrated or varied a language model’s output distribution becomes during reinforcement learning. Existing findings point in opposing directions: increasing entropy can support exploration, while decreasing it can improve performance. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation for why either intervention can help.

The proposed explanation centers on Entropy Discrepancy, a distributional divergence between positive and negative samples. The theoretical framework shows that this quantity governs the effect of entropy control. From that analysis, the authors derive a dynamic schedule that adjusts the entropy coefficient as training progresses, switching between encouraging and discouraging entropy.

Experiments confirm a correlation between Entropy Discrepancy and the effectiveness of entropy interventions. The adaptive schedule improves Pass@K by a reported 6.7% on AIME24 and 17.52% on puzzle tasks compared with vanilla reinforcement learning, while outperforming recent reasoning methods in the evaluation. The contribution is a principled basis for adapting entropy control to the evolving training distribution, connecting apparently conflicting empirical recommendations.
icml-2026-demystifying-entropy-control-i.tldr: A distribution-based measure guides when to increase or decrease entropy during language-model reinforcement learning, improving reported reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning fine-tuning can make a language model’s responses less diverse. Existing interventions often trade correctness against variety, and their effects can vary across tasks. This paper develops a theoretical account of the problem, proving how selection and reinforcement bias produce the collapse in diversity.

The analysis identifies a more targeted intervention: reward modifications intended to address diversity collapse only need to affect correct trajectories. The authors build differential smoothing around this observation. Within their theoretical analysis, the method improves both correctness and diversity, and is universally superior to the alternatives considered. The same framework characterizes when existing heuristics help and why they fail.

Experiments cover models with 1B to 7B parameters and tasks including CountDown and real-world mathematical reasoning. They report consistent improvements in both Pass@1 and Pass@k, with gains of up to 6.7% on AIME24. Together, the theory and experiments support preserving a broader range of successful reasoning trajectories while also improving answer correctness.
icml-2026-differential-smoothing-mitigat.tldr: Differential smoothing targets rewards on correct trajectories to improve both reasoning accuracy and output diversity during reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Sparse autoencoders decompose a neural network’s activations into features intended to be understandable to people. A single autoencoder, however, captures only part of the feature structure available in those activations. This paper studies whether combining several sparse autoencoders can provide a more useful representation.

The authors formalize ensembles and develop two approaches. Naive bagging combines autoencoders trained from different random initializations. Boosting trains them sequentially so that later models focus on reconstruction errors left by earlier ones. Theoretical analysis justifies both approaches as ways to reduce reconstruction error, connecting the ensemble design to a concrete representational objective.

Experiments span three combinations of language models and autoencoder architectures. Against a single expanded autoencoder with the same total number of features, ensembles improve activation reconstruction and stability. They also perform better on concept detection and removal of spurious correlations. These comparisons indicate that organizing features across multiple autoencoders can offer practical benefits beyond simply increasing the feature count of one model.
icml-2026-ensembling-sparse-autoencoders.tldr: Combining sparse autoencoders improves reconstruction, stability, and downstream utility compared with a single autoencoder containing the same number of features.

paragraphs: Generating large graphs requires modeling both their connections and the features attached to their nodes and edges. Hierarchical methods improve scalability, but often leave those features out. The challenge also applies to hypergraphs, whose relationships can connect more than two entities and therefore represent higher-order structure.

FAHNES generates topology and features together through a hierarchy of scales. It builds these representations using node coarsening and localized expansion. A hierarchical scale encoding controls the granularity of the representation and maintains consistency across scales. This makes feature generation part of the same multiscale process that constructs the connections.

The authors evaluate the framework on synthetic data, 3D meshes, and graph point clouds, reporting competitive or state-of-the-art performance. They also report distinctive scalability to large graphs and hypergraphs that include features. The approach matters because structural size and descriptive richness are handled within one generative framework, extending the scope of hierarchical generation to data where connectivity alone is insufficient.
icml-2026-feature-aware-hyper-graph-gene.tldr: FAHNES jointly generates connections and features across scales, supporting large featured graphs and hypergraphs with strong reported performance.

paragraphs: Choosing a large gradient-descent step while retaining convergence is difficult when a training objective lacks a global smoothness bound. This paper introduces a unified definition of large steps requiring only local Lipschitz, or even Hölder, continuity of the gradient. That broadens the analysis to objectives beyond the globally smooth setting.

The authors design adaptive first-order methods that provably produce large steps and operate at the edge of stability from the beginning of training. Their loss can fluctuate as it decreases, while step size multiplied by sharpness stays above the threshold of two. Here, sharpness is measured by the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian.

The method can also drive sharpness to its global minimum. However, the authors find that reaching globally flat regions too early may slow convergence and harm generalization. Using a self-stabilization argument, they permit movement into slightly sharper valleys and improve previously unsuccessful training runs. The findings connect convergence behavior to when and how training encounters flat regions.
icml-2026-flatland-the-adventures-of-gra.tldr: Adaptive large-step gradient methods reveal that reaching extremely flat regions too early can impede convergence and generalization.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders use latent variables to represent data, but their role in generalization has been difficult to characterize theoretically. Existing analyses have largely addressed supervised learning or discrete latent spaces. This paper develops an information-theoretic treatment for the continuous latent variables used in standard variational autoencoders.

The authors adapt the leave-one-out conditional mutual information framework from supervised learning to this unsupervised setting. Their resulting generalization bound depends solely on the information complexity of the encoder and latent variables, without a decoder-dependent term. This identifies the quantities controlling the derived bound and gives the encoder and latent representation a central role in the analysis.

The framework also extends to hierarchical variational autoencoders, where it produces bounds for individual layers. For data generation, the authors derive a bound on the 2-Wasserstein distance between the true and generated distributions. These extensions connect the same information-theoretic principles to both generalization and distributional fidelity, expanding the analysis beyond a single latent-layer model.
icml-2026-information-theoretic-generali.tldr: New VAE generalization bounds depend on encoder and latent-variable information complexity, with extensions to hierarchical models and generated distributions.

paragraphs: Editing a generative model’s intermediate representations can steer its behavior, but successful interventions have outpaced their theoretical explanation. This paper develops a framework for concept steering through affine transformations. Its aim is to explain how concepts can be removed or changed while controlling disturbance to the representation.

The authors first connect a standard behavior-removal approach to LEACE, a closed-form method for affine concept erasure, proving that the former is a special case. They then introduce LEACE-Switch for concept switching and characterize assumptions under which it yields an optimal affine solution. This separates the mathematical guarantee from the conditions needed to obtain it.

MidSteer extends the analysis into a more general framework that relaxes those assumptions and supports directed transformations with minimal disturbance. Experiments report favorable performance across tasks, modalities, and architectures, including vision diffusion models and language models. The contribution combines a theory of existing steering operations with a broader method for manipulating concepts across different kinds of generative systems.
icml-2026-midsteer-optimal-affine-framew.tldr: MidSteer develops affine concept steering with minimal disturbance, extending a theory linking behavior removal, concept erasure, and concept switching.

paragraphs: Pretrained weights are usually treated as the starting point for further optimization. This paper instead views pretraining as producing a distribution over parameter vectors that already contains task-specific experts. The central question becomes how densely useful specialists populate the neighborhood around the pretrained model.

The authors show that expert solutions occupy a negligible fraction of this distribution for smaller or insufficiently trained models. In that setting, finding them relies on structured optimization such as gradient descent. For large, well-pretrained models, they find a much higher density: diverse specialists occupy a substantial portion of the nearby parameter space.

Motivated by this distinction, the paper explores sampling N parameter vectors randomly, selecting the best K, and combining their predictions by majority vote. Sampling is fully parallel, and the vote brings together complementary expertise. For contemporary large-scale models, the approach is competitive with PPO, GRPO, and ES. The finding ties this simple post-training strategy to the density of experts associated with model scale and pretraining quality.
icml-2026-neural-thickets-diverse-task-e.tldr: Large, well-pretrained models contain dense nearby task experts that can be sampled, selected, and ensembled competitively with standard post-training methods.

paragraphs: Density-based anomaly detection identifies unusual data through its estimated probability density. Noise from measurement conditions or the surrounding environment can distort that estimate and degrade predictions. NRDE aims to isolate this nuisance variation so that anomaly decisions reflect the sources generating the underlying data.

The method learns a normalizing flow with Jacobian regularization to estimate the data’s sources, even though the generating process is unknown. It divides those sources into two groups: one responsible for pure data and another responsible for noise. It then generates pure data and uses its density to detect anomalies attributable to the pure-data sources.

This separation is the basis of the method’s claimed noise robustness, and the paper supplies theoretical results supporting its effectiveness. The evaluation compares NRDE with 17 baselines across 47 datasets, covering ordinary detection, anomaly contamination, noisy data, and transductive outlier detection. These settings examine the approach under several distinct detection conditions; the abstract establishes the evaluation’s breadth without specifying numerical comparative outcomes.
icml-2026-noise-robust-density-estimatio.tldr: NRDE separates estimated data and noise sources to base tabular anomaly detection on the density of underlying pure data.

paragraphs: When each observation is a probability distribution, PCA can be performed by embedding distributions into a Hilbert space. In practice, each distribution is itself observed through samples. This paper studies the resulting two-level estimation problem: learning from n distributions when only m samples are available from each.

The authors derive convergence rates of n^{-1/2} + m^{-α} for the empirical covariance operator and PCA excess risk, with α determined by the embedding. The two terms distinguish uncertainty from having finitely many distributions from uncertainty in estimating each distribution. Their balance explains a transition between sparse and dense sampling regimes.

In the dense regime, the empirical covariance error achieves a minimax-optimal rate. Numerical experiments support the theoretical rates and show that suitable subsampling can preserve PCA accuracy while reducing computation. The practical implication is that collecting or processing more samples within each distribution has a benefit governed by the other source of uncertainty: how many distributions are available overall.
icml-2026-pca-of-probability-measures-sp.tldr: The paper quantifies how PCA accuracy depends jointly on the number of distributions and the samples available from each.

paragraphs: Solving a partial differential equation from partial observations requires combining measurements with the physical relationships governing the solution. Physics-informed spectral diffusion learns a joint distribution over equation parameters and solutions, enabling generation conditioned on available observations. The formulation includes both forward and inverse PDE problems.

The diffusion process operates in a latent space of scaled spectral representations. This reduces dimensionality relative to grid-based diffusion and makes Gaussian noise correspond to functions with controlled regularity. That property keeps the induced function-space process within a class where the relevant PDE operators are mathematically well defined.

During inference, the method combines diffusion posterior sampling with Adam-based updates at every diffusion step to impose physics and measurement constraints. Tests on Poisson, Helmholtz, and incompressible Navier–Stokes equations report better accuracy and computational efficiency than existing diffusion-based PDE solvers. The contribution connects the mathematical suitability of the representation with observation-conditioned generation, allowing physical constraints to guide the sampling process rather than relying on learned distributions alone.
icml-2026-physics-informed-diffusion-mod.tldr: Spectral-space diffusion combines learned PDE distributions with inference-time physics constraints to improve solution accuracy and computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning must learn from existing data without gathering new experience. In safety-critical settings, a high average return is insufficient if a policy also produces disastrous outcomes. RAMAC targets this lower-tail risk while retaining an expressive policy capable of representing multiple distinct action patterns.

The framework combines a generative actor, such as a diffusion or flow model, with a distributional critic. Its objective joins Conditional Value-at-Risk, which emphasizes poor outcomes, with behavioral cloning. The latter keeps the learned behavior closer to the recorded data. An objective-level analysis shows that controlling this divergence suppresses out-of-distribution actions and stabilizes the risk objective.

The authors instantiate RAMAC with a diffusion actor, illustrate the mechanism on a two-dimensional risky bandit, and evaluate it on Stochastic-D4RL. They observe consistent gains in CVaR at the 0.1 level while maintaining strong returns. These results support combining expressive policies with behavior regularization to improve lower-tail outcomes without abandoning the objective of achieving useful overall performance.
icml-2026-ramac-multimodal-risk-aware-of.tldr: RAMAC combines expressive generative policies, lower-tail risk optimization, and behavioral cloning to improve risk-sensitive offline reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: A model soup combines the parameters of several models adapted from a common starting model into one model. Existing recipes have relied on supervised learning with a shared loss on labeled data. Self-Soupervision extends the approach to self-supervised learning, allowing unlabeled data to shape the models being combined.

Self-Souping can adapt ingredients to a new task’s unlabeled data or to data reflecting a distribution shift. In one reported procedure, the models use corrupted test data before being fine-tuned back on uncorrupted training data. This improves robustness by 3.5% on ImageNet-C and 7% on LAION-C, connecting unlabeled adaptation with resilience to corruption.

The paper also demonstrates that ingredients can differ in their self-supervised hyperparameters and even their learning algorithms. Soups combining MAE, MoCoV3, MMCR, and LeJEPA ingredients are more accurate than any individual ingredient in the reported experiments. This expands the sources of useful diversity available for parameter averaging, beyond models trained with the same supervised objective.
icml-2026-self-soupervision-cooking-mode.tldr: Self-Soupervision extends parameter-averaged model soups to unlabeled adaptation and mixtures of different self-supervised learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Predicting a vessel’s position far into the future is difficult because uncertainty compounds across navigation decisions and environmental influences. A trajectory may remain locally plausible yet gradually drift away from a coherent overall direction. SKETCH addresses this by incorporating a higher-level representation of navigational intent.

The framework conditions future motion on a Next Key Point, a semantic target that guides the trajectory. This divides the prediction problem into global decision-making and local motion modeling. Conditioning on that target restricts possible trajectories to semantically feasible subsets, giving the local predictions a shared directional reference over the longer horizon.

A pretraining and fine-tuning strategy estimates the prior over the next key point from historical observations. Experiments on real-world AIS data report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art approaches, especially for long travel durations, directional accuracy, and detailed trajectory prediction. The findings support separating inferred intent from local movement as a way to maintain global coherence while predicting the finer structure of vessel motion.
icml-2026-sketch-semantic-key-point-cond.tldr: SKETCH conditions vessel trajectories on an inferred semantic next key point to improve long-horizon direction and motion prediction.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models must act using visual inputs that may differ from their training experience. This paper systematically studies unseen visual disturbances and finds substantial performance degradation in recent models. Since training data cannot cover every possible disturbance, it investigates filtering potentially disruptive visual information within the model.

The proposed Information Bottleneck Adapter is a lightweight module grounded in information theory. It selectively filters potential noise from visual inputs without requiring additional data or augmentation. The authors report an average improvement of 30% over the baseline while adding fewer than 10 million parameters, making the intervention small relative to the evaluated backbones.

StableVLA also achieves robustness competitive with 7B-scale models using a 0.5B backbone, despite lacking pretraining on Open X-Embodiment. The approach preserves accuracy on long-horizon tasks and surpasses OpenPi under real-world visual disturbances. These findings support selective visual filtering as an efficient route to robustness, with the reported gains tied to the disturbances and tasks examined in the study.
icml-2026-stablevla-towards-robust-visio.tldr: A small information-bottleneck adapter improves vision-language-action robustness to unseen visual disturbances without extra data or augmentation.

paragraphs: Online learning becomes difficult when the environment changes repeatedly. Methods designed around confidently detecting a single change may perform poorly when changes occur multiple times. This paper identifies a failure mechanism called endogenous confounding and shows that classical methods can consequently suffer high regret.

The proposed Anytime Tracking CUSUM algorithms use selective detection. They balance ignoring small changes that are difficult to distinguish from uncertainty against responding quickly to significant shifts. They are horizon-free, meaning the algorithm does not require a predetermined endpoint for the learning process. This makes repeated adaptation central to the design.

For a properly tuned algorithm, the authors prove regret close to a new information-theoretic lower bound on what any learner can achieve in the multiple-change setting. This establishes nearly minimax-optimal performance under the stated tuning requirement. Synthetic and real-world experiments support the theoretical findings. The result explains why detecting every shift with high confidence is not the sole organizing principle for effective learning in repeatedly changing environments.
icml-2026-the-cost-of-learning-under-mul.tldr: Anytime Tracking CUSUM selectively responds to significant changes and achieves nearly minimax-optimal regret when properly tuned.

paragraphs: Looped Transformers repeatedly refine a token’s internal representation, but extra processing can sometimes turn a correct prediction into an error. This paper calls that behavior latent overthinking. An oracle iteration policy reveals potential gains of up to 7.3%, motivating a learned mechanism for deciding which tokens need more processing.

Think-at-Hard uses a lightweight neural decider to identify tokens likely to be wrong after the standard pass. Depth-aware LoRA modules then specialize additional iterations toward refining those difficult tokens. A duo-causal attention mechanism allows information to flow across both token positions and iteration depths while retaining full sequential parallelism.

Across nine math, question-answering, and coding benchmarks, equal-parameter models outperform always-iterate baselines by 3.8–4.4% while skipping iterations on 93% of tokens. They also exceed single-iteration Qwen3 baselines by 3.0–3.8%. Allowing less than 3% additional parameters produces larger gains. The results support allocating refinement selectively, with improved accuracy accompanying much less frequent iteration in the evaluated models.
icml-2026-think-at-hard-dynamic-looped-t.tldr: Think-at-Hard improves reasoning by selectively refining difficult tokens, avoiding extra iterations that can overturn correct predictions.

paragraphs: Video understanding can require domain knowledge and reasoning beyond recognizing visible objects or actions. VideoKR addresses this through a training corpus designed specifically for those demands. It contains 315,000 reasoning examples drawn from 145,000 newly collected, Creative Commons-licensed videos covering expert domains.

The authors develop a human-in-the-loop generation pipeline organized around reasoning skills and progressively deeper capabilities. It targets difficulty, diversity, and reliability in both questions and their reasoning rationales. They also introduce VideoKR-Eval, an expert-annotated benchmark designed so that answering requires understanding the video and applying knowledge rather than exploiting textual shortcuts.

Using supervised fine-tuning followed by GRPO, models trained on VideoKR outperform prior post-training approaches on knowledge-intensive video reasoning while remaining competitive on general video reasoning. Ablation studies examine the corpus’s contributions. The findings identify data design as a substantial contributor to progress: the training examples explicitly exercise the kinds of knowledge and reasoning that the accompanying evaluation is designed to test.
icml-2026-videokr-towards-knowledge-and-.tldr: VideoKR provides expert-domain video reasoning data and evaluation that improve knowledge-intensive understanding under a standard post-training pipeline.

paragraphs: Estimating scene flow from 4D radar means recovering how the observed scene moves, but obtaining ground-truth motion labels is difficult. Radar measurements also provide weak signals for self-supervised learning. This paper develops an iterative training framework that uses images and vehicle odometry as auxiliary supervision, avoiding LiDAR-based label generation.

Off-the-shelf image tracking and segmentation produce tracked object masks, which are projected into three-dimensional space. These masks provide instance-level guidance for two self-supervised losses. For static regions, a separate rigid-motion loss combines vehicle odometry with motion information intrinsic to radar. The framework thus uses different supervisory cues for object instances and static surroundings.

On the real-world View-of-Delft dataset, the method outperforms leading cross-modal approaches that derive supervision from dense LiDAR tracking. It also surpasses existing fully supervised scene-flow methods in the reported evaluation. The result shows that carefully structured image and odometry supervision can be effective for radar motion learning, even against approaches supported by richer sensors or explicit labels.
icml-2026-weakly-supervised-cross-modal-.tldr: An iterative radar scene-flow method uses image-derived object guidance and odometry to outperform LiDAR-supervised and fully supervised approaches on View-of-Delft.
